articleTitle: Session 1: Industrial, University and cate training: Preparing the engineer for the microprocessor era
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The impact of the microprocessor on the engineering world is just beginning to be felt in South Africa. In the United Kingdom and the USA the engineer has been left in no doubt as to the importance of this product of technological innovation. In virtually every field of engineering and science the microprocessor is finding applications. The reason for this becomes clear when the basic role of the engineer is examined. In every field where he applies his skills, the problems which he solves require the processing of information — information which may be gained in a variety of ways, but from from which ‘output’ information must be derived. It is within these areas that the microprocessor is invaluable, as never before has the engineer had available such a cheap, but capable, information-processing facility.

articleTitle: Technical potential in Africa: Mining and development in Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I would like to start by stating that I believe everyone in Africa wants development. The benefits of development arc clear to everyone who looks — they are freedom from hunger and disease, from ignorance and want, and from a host of other quantifiable and non-quantifiable things. But they all boil down to a simple, very quantifiable thing — longevity. The fact is that people in developed states tend to live longer, and long life is attractive<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">(1)</sup>. Secondly, I believe that it is very dangerous to talk of ‘appropriate technology’ as a panacea of developmental ills. There is a very real risk that ‘appropriate technology’, which is generally understood as being labour intensive, low capital ventures in a developing economy, may not be in the least appropriate to such an economy. A simple example will suffice — a petrochemical plant is normally thought to be one of the most capital intensive of all such works, yet if the products of such a plant remain within the economy of the country in which it is built, the marketing and use of those products spawn thousands of peripheral, low capital investment jobs. (Automobile maintenance, petrol sales, plastics fabrication, hard-surfacing of roads etc).

articleTitle: Environmental standards and their implications in power utility engineering Twenty-sixth Bernard Price Memorial Lecture
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The increasingly stringent and wideranging environmental standards being set in the world today pose many problems for the power utility engineer in design of his works. This paper briefly reviews such standards in the principal areas of air, water and noise, and indicates how an ultra-conservative approach to the protection of the environment is placing a significant cost burden on power utilities, and thereby onto the community. It questions the validity of many of the standards and the basis for environmental control and emphasises the necessity for the engineering profession to be involved in the determination of rational standards.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A realization of the advantages of electricity as a source of power motivated many industries and municipalities, at the turn of the century, to invest in their own power plants. It was soon appreciated, however, that centralized large generating stations could provide electricity more cheaply than numerous small installations. The advent of high voltage ac transmission gave further impetus to the establishment of centralized stations since these could be located remotely from the utilization centres. This enabled the stations to be constructed in regions where there were plentiful supplies of coal and water. The cost advantages of burning cheap low grade fuel and the elimination of expensive transportation were fully exploited leading to large scale reductions in electricity tariffs.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This paper describes the manner in which induction heating of an oil pipeline was accomplished at Richards Bay. An equivalent circuit for the pipeline configuration is deduced, and techniques for determining the values of components in the circuit for unsaturated and saturated magnetic conditions are given. Predictions are compared with measurements made on the pipeline.

abstract: In reply to Mr Baker the successful application of SF<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sub> as an insulant has naturally led to consideration of its use in transformers. There is however a fundamental difference in that the oil in a transformer performs the dual function of acting as an insulator and as a heat transfer medium. SF<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sub> can be used in transformers, but because of its relatively poor performance for heat transfer purposes, the transformer has to be designed with much lower thermal loading than a conventional oil-filled unit and therefore becomes prohibitively expensive.

articleTitle: Technical potential in Africa: The industrialization of Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Africa, often referred to in the past as the slumbering giant, has been roused from its long sleep. This is a reality which has to be faced. The winds of change which have blown over the continent during the past two decades have not only brought an end to what has been termed the colonial era, but have indeed changed the face of Africa. There was an outcry for independence, and new states emerged almost overnight. Unfortunately newly won political independence in the majority of cases did not go hand in hand with economic and social freedom and stability. This is borne out by the fact that while Africa, with a total population of 391 million (1974 figure), constituting about 10 per cent of world population, has a share of only about 0,5 per cent in world production. South Africa, on the other hand, with only 6 per cent of Africa's population, is responsible for about 42 per cent of its industrial production.
